==Problem==
The figure below shows a tiling of <imath> 1 \times 1 </imath> unit squares. Each row of unit squares is shifted horizontally by half a unit relative to the row above it. A shaded square is drawn on top of the tiling. Each vertex of the shaded square is a vertex of one of the unit squares. In square units, what is the area of the shaded square?

[[File:2026 amc 8 q13.png | 650px]]

<cmath>\textbf{A. } 10 \quad \textbf{B. }  \frac{21}{2}  \quad \textbf{C. }  \frac{32}{3}  \quad \textbf{D. } 11 \quad \textbf{E. } \frac{34}{3}  </cmath>

==Solution==

Label the vertices <imath> A </imath>, <imath> B </imath>, <imath> C </imath>, <imath> D </imath>, in clockwise order. Then, we use coordinate geometry to easily solve this. Let point <imath> A </imath> be on <imath> (0, 0) </imath>. Then, point <imath> B </imath> is 1 unit up and 3 right of <imath> (0, 0) </imath>, or <imath> (3, 1) </imath>. The figure is said to be a square. and so we just calculate the distance from <imath> (0, 0) </imath> to <imath> (1, 3) </imath>. Using the distance formula, we have <imath> \sqrt{(1-0)^2 + (3-0)^2} = \sqrt{(1+9)} = \sqrt{10} </imath>. The area is just this value squared, or <imath>\boxed{10}</imath>.

~Pinotation

==Solution 2==
Since the side length of a square is 1 unit, we can use Pythagoras on a side length (note that we only need to find one side since the shape is a square). If we do it on the left side, we get <imath>\sqrt{3^2+(0.5+0.5)^2}=\sqrt{10}</imath>. Therefore, the final area is the side length squared, which is <imath>(\sqrt{10})^2=\boxed{\textbf{(A) }10}</imath>. ~Baihly2024

==Solution 3==
Notice that the top-left side of our square is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs of length <imath>1</imath>cm and <imath>3</imath>cm. Using the Pythagorean Theorem, the side length of our square is <imath>\sqrt{1^2+3^2}=\sqrt{10}</imath>cm, so the area is <imath>\sqrt{10}^2=10</imath>cm<imath>^2</imath>, so we obtain <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) }10}</imath>.

~Yuhao2012

==Solution 4(Quick And Easy)==
Notice that we can construct a 4x4 square that passes tangent to each corner. The area of this square is 16. This square forms 4 congruent right triangles, with a base of 3 and height of 1. The area of one of these triangles is 1.5, and you can multiply that by 4 to get the total area of these triangles, 6. Subtract that from the area of the constructed square to get <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) }10}</imath>. as your answer.

==Solution 5==

Similar to Solution 4, we construct one right triangle outside the square. We can see that it has side lengths 3 and 1. Using the Pythagorean Theorem we find that the hypotenuse, which is also a side of the original square, is <imath>\sqrt{10}</imath>. Now, we can find the area of the square by squaring that, which yields <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) }10}</imath>.

~Lightning_Fox

==Solution 6 (Without Pythagoras or Distance Formula)==

*Note: this solution is unreliable and only use it if you have no other methods to solve.
We can count the number of small squares inside the large square and add <imath>1</imath> to our running count if the square is more than half shaded, add <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath> if it is exactly (or almost exactly) <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath> shaded, and add <imath>0</imath> if it is less than half shaded. Counting the squares, we have <imath>5</imath> fully shaded, <imath>4</imath> more than half, and <imath>2</imath> exactly half. <imath>5+4+2\times{\frac{1}{2}}=\boxed{\textbf{(A)} 10}</imath>

~jeremyq
